articles.title: Op-Ed: From the Bargaining Table to Olympia, Educators Need Our Support Now
articles.author: Kelabe Tewolde
paras: It’s the last few weeks of the summer. Everyone is trying to fit in one last trip out of town, hosting cookouts, spending evenings at the lake, or like many parents diving into back to school shopping. Usually educators are gearing up and preparing to welcome back students to the classroom, but this year there is a bit of a road block.

Between now and September 2nd, the first day of school, members of Seattle Education Association (SEA) are bargaining from 9am to 9pm with Seattle Public Schools (SPS) for a fair contract. That was until last night (August 29th), when SPS walked away from the bargaining table as talks broke down regarding cuts to special education.

On August 26th, SEA authorized a strike. This doesn’t necessarily mean they will strike, but SEA’s bargaining team has the greenlight. With the district walking away from the bargaining table it is increasingly likely SEA will have their third strike in 11 years. We are just a few days away from the start of the school year, and you may be asking, “What’s the hold up?”

SEA has agreed to 12 of 57 issues and struggle to find common ground on what holds the most weight in these negotiations, centering the experience of their students and members. They have found that pressurization and wages are where the district and SEA are unable to come to an agreement. You may be wondering, what this actually means. Teachers are focused on pressurization, a.k.a. increased workload. Pressurization comes in the forms of increases in caseload, class size, and other demands that take their time and focus away from students and lead to educator burnout.

When we constantly put more and more on our educators' plates, we limit the time and energy they have to actually teach our children. And when we talk about wages, we mean making sure all SPS employees can afford to live in the city where they work. In a city as expensive as Seattle, many of the lower-paid workers are finding it difficult to afford to live here in the communities they serve. Educators are not looking for a massive raise in this contract. It is simply a cost-of-living adjustment that will ease the burden of affordability.
If I were to simplify that for the everyday person not at the bargaining table: Teachers want to improve working conditions because their working conditions are their students' learning conditions.
SEA is digging into the district’s annual $1.3 billion budget and finding that part of the problem is state funding. And part of the problem is misplaced priorities.
What is SEA fighting for beyond pressurization and wages?

Special education students have a civil right to a high-quality education : That means we need to meet their individual education plan (IEP). With more students with IEPs in general education, SPS needs to ensure that the co-teaching models are effective. Teachers need an opportunity and space in their schedule to collaborate and help ALL of their students succeed. In these co-teaching models, SPS needs to have a plan to fill in for vacancies and leaves so students with IEPs have teachers with a Special Education endorsement. This is not only an issue around providing a high quality education for all our students, but it is a civil rights issue.

Reasonable class sizes: This is critical to how students succeed. Currently, SEA’s contract includes overage pay as an incentive for the district to keep class sizes a reasonable size, but we are hearing from educators that they don’t want that overage pay. On a personal note, my friend that teaches in a different district similarly had overage pay for having a large class. Mid-year, she had to advocate to split the class up because the learning environment in a class of 35 students was not conducive to student success.

Smaller class sizes give educators the ability to connect with students and help them succeed. SEA states: “We need to create a true cap, beyond which the district must add staff or reduce the class size to ensure students have the opportunity to learn.”
Beyond class sizes, SEA has a variety of other proposals that include safety, AI usage in the classroom, and substitute reimbursement.
Long term, we need solutions from the state
These issues could be solved at the state level if we had a legislature that would prioritize the learning conditions of our children.

In 2014, we had the opportunity to implement smaller class sizes through I-1351 , providing students with one-on-one attention from caring and qualified teachers and support staff. While voters backed smaller class sizes, the state legislature unfortunately left the initiative unfunded, and in 2015 the state legislature delayed its implementation. Eventually in 2017, the legislature repealed the cap on class sizes, due to a lack of funding, leading us to the mess we are in now: Large class sizes, teachers without the resources to effectively serve their students, and students failed by a system that they simply inherited.

Teachers are burnt out and it reflects in how many educators are leaving our schools. One special education teacher told me that: “Last year was the worst teacher year of my life due to an unsustainable and unsupported SpEd caseload. And every SpEd teacher in my building except one left at the end of last year. It’s leading to massive burnout and attrition.”
Without proper class sizes and support, we are failing our teachers, and in turn failing our children.
Many critics to this solution will bring up, “if smaller class sizes were unfunded in 2014, how would you fund them now, especially with an upcoming austerity budget?”

Well, simply put, we would need to reform our tax code like WEA recommended about a decade ago. I’m writing this off the heels of Washington State coming in as No. 1 — for corporate tax breaks and corporations like Microsoft paying a tax rate of 2.4%, while people that earn less than $33,500 a year have a tax rate of 13.8% . We need a legislature that is bold enough to stand up for our values and provide a quality education for all, while creating a sensible tax code that makes everyone pay their fair share .

And this November, we have a choice in legislative races all over the state. We need to elect legislators that are willing to balance the tax code. We deserve legislators who will stand with workers over corporate profits. And legislators that support our educators all year long, not just during an election year.

In the upcoming days, I ask you to support our teachers. This could be showing up for the bargaining team at rallies, spreading the word via social media, calling on the district to meet SEA’s proposals , and, if there is a strike, picketing with teachers throughout the city demanding SPS meet their proposals.

articles.title: PONGO POETRY | A Cold Sun
paras: Were you there when I lost one of my teeth? Were you there when I made a friend? Were you there when I finished my blueprints of the stuff I like to build?
Where were you when I got hurt? How long are you going to be gone? Will I miss anything?
I want you to know that I forgive you. For all the times you made me cry. For every time you yelled at me. For the times you scared me.
I hope you and your new kids Are happy with the life you have. I like to think you haven't forgotten about me Even though it may not be true.
I don't know if you know this, but I'm sixteen. I changed my name. It might be a different name soon.

I want you there when I graduate from high school. I want you there with me when I walk down the aisle of my wedding. You mean so much to me But I mean so little to you. And that's fine. You keep living your life and I'll live mine.

Oh! T* has just finished college. She will be able to start teaching in two years. And she is still with B*. They are now living together And will move close to Mom. And I'm pansexual — I love people based on their personality Not their gender or looks.
* Names redacted to protect youth confidentiality.
You took everything I needed and never gave it back
I needed love but you made it so I couldn't even love myself
I needed education but you wouldn't let me leave the house
I needed safety but you let my siblings go unsupervised
I needed comfort but you caused me to hide in my room
I needed a mom but you wouldn't even give that to me
you were supposed to be my sun yet I am still so Cold.

Pongo Poetry Project's mission is to engage youth in writing poetry to inspire healing and growth. For over 20 years, Pongo has mentored poetry with children at the Child Study Treatment Center (CSTC), the only state-run psychiatric hospital for youth in Washington State. Many CSTC youth are coping with severe emotional, behavioral, and mental health challenges. Approximately 40% of youth arrive at CSTC having been court ordered to get treatment; however, by the end of their stay, most youth residents become voluntary participants.

Pongo believes there is power in creative expression, and articulating one's pain to an empathetic audience. Through this special monthly column in partnership with the South Seattle Emerald, Pongo invites readers to bear witness to the pain, resilience, and creative capacity of youth whose voices and perspectives are too often relegated to the periphery. To learn more about how Pongo inspires healing and relief in youth coping with mental and emotional turmoil, register for " What Words Can Hold ," its fall community poetry writing night!

articles.title: ‘Grassroots will beat big money every day’: can a DSA member flip a Republican Senate seat?
articles.author: David Smith in Washington
paras: Angie Nixon won one of the biggest upsets in US midterm primaries – and if elected, the Democrat would be the first African American senator in Florida history

The Democratic establishment had the money, the machinery and the candidate with national name recognition. Angie Nixon had a bookshop called Café Resistance and a grassroots campaign for the Senate. On primary election night in Florida , Nixon won in arguably the biggest upset of the primary season. But at least one person was not shocked: Angie Nixon herself. “We weren’t surprised,” the 42-year-old reflects after overcoming a vast fundraising disadvantage to defeat Alex Vindman , a combat veteran who testified against Donald Trump during his first impeachment. “We actually knew we were going to win; we just didn’t know that we were going to win by that much. We put in the work and so super excited about the outcome. It shows that good old-fashioned grassroots organising will beat big money each and every day.”

Nixon won 56.1% of the vote to Vindman’s 43.9%. The result stirred tensions within the Democratic party in a year defined by the struggle between moderates and economic populists . In Florida – a state that has trended increasingly Republican in recent years and is now Trump’s home state – Democrats have now nominated a member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) who speaks openly about class war.

articles.title: The datacenter backlash is bringing the entire political spectrum together – against Big Tech billionaires
articles.author: Aaron Regunberg
paras: The movement against datacenters is uniting Americans because they perfectly illustrate how a few individuals hold all the power to control decisions that impact our lives

Bryce Gustafson has been knocking on doors in Indiana for more than a decade. The lead organizer with Citizens Action Coalition (CAC), a consumer and environmental organization, he usually encounters a mix of reactions when he’s out canvassing; whatever issue he’s talking about, there’s always at least a few people on the other side. But at a recent festival in the rural town of Monrovia, Indiana, he was struck by an unusual spirit of unity.

He was there about a proposed datacenter , a 550-acre (222-hectare) Google project in this small town of 1,600 people. “I had 50 people I talked to,” Gustafson told me. “Nobody wanted that datacenter in their community. And at least a half a dozen people came up to me to say, ‘Hey, I voted for Trump. What the heck’s he doing, supporting these things?’”

articles.title: Bill Gates in his own words: How he’s using AI, and why he’s worried about the future
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: This week on the GeekWire Podcast: Bill Gates published a new essay warning that the AI industry is crossing the safety lines it set for itself, and that nobody is preparing for what’s coming . At age 70, he also uses AI more than most people half his age, and he finds it enthralling, as you’ll hear on this week’s show, with highlights from our interview with him.
Along the way, we dig into his three proposals: new institutions for managing the transition, a category of jobs reserved for humans, and a tax on the use and purchase of AI and robots.

The change in his own tech usage: “I joke with people that I used to have Claude-like people that I would send email to, but they were so slow, and there were some topics they didn’t actually know. … It’s three a.m. I want to understand sodium batteries, and now there’s no reason to go to sleep. Here we go. Yeah, it’s crazy.”

How he uses AI specifically: “If you’re a curious person, this is a mind-blowing time. When I’m working on malaria, nutrition, my poor humans that I work with always get these long conversations from me, where I paste in — me, Claude, me, ChatGPT. Sometimes I do it if there’s three of us: Claude, ChatGPT and me, debating these things.”

On where personal agents are headed: “We will get to a point where you won’t buy things yourself. You just won’t. … You won’t go to those applications. You’ll just go to your personal agent. … From a productivity point of view, we are in heaven.”

What has surprised him: “I was shocked by ChatGPT, and I was shocked by Claude Code. Those are both things where I went, oh my God. … I did not expect that a statistical machine would essentially learn to read, and the idea that the code is better than human code. Those are two stunning thresholds.”

On writing this essay: “It’s very unnatural for me to think that innovation may be a net negative if it’s not managed properly. The more I wrote the memo, the more I was like, Jesus, we really need to get our act together here. Even though this may come across as negative, that’s the truth. If we don’t step up, the negatives will substantially outweigh the positives.”

What AI leaders say privately: “You’re in this perverse period right now where people in the AI industry who are willing to say that AI might have some negative effects are told, ‘Hey, you’re hurting our PR while we’re trying to raise trillions of dollars.’ … I know they’re all worried. Or all of them that I know, which is basically everybody but Elon.”

On losing control of AI: “The wake-up for the memo is that the bad stuff thresholds are all being crossed. Even lack of control that I thought would be many years from now, we’re seeing lack of control. … These are people who are super expert on the thing, going, well, maybe we won’t be able to control these things. What kind of risk have we chosen to run here?”

On how fast robots are coming: “What’s weird about AI is it’s better at doing jobs across the entire economy, including physical jobs when the robots come — which you can guess when that is, but my view is it’s only a couple of years.”

Is he still an optimist? “I don’t think being pessimistic is helpful. I do think, wow, this is sure an interesting time. I’m the guy who in my 30s thought people in their 50s or 60s didn’t understand anything. So it’s kind of bizarre if a guy who’s 70 comes and writes a memo that’s actually helpful. … But I am very concerned. And honestly, when you get people one-on-one, so are they.”

articles.title: Op-Ed: Washington’s Primary Election Results Underscore the Case for Proportional Ranked Choice Voting
articles.author: Zane Gustafson
paras: From Seattle to Spokane and everywhere in between, August’s primary results show an electorate yearning for more options, and proportional ranked choice voting is the way to make viable candidates from outside the two-party system.

Contrary to the blinkered two-party analysis in the Seattle Times , which explicitly excluded independent candidates and ignored major differences between Democrats, Washington primary voters showed they support three viable statewide political parties: Democrats (40% of the statewide Congressional primary vote), Republicans (35%), and an emerging left-wing party (20%).

For this analysis, I analyzed candidate websites for rhetoric and policy platforms to identify which candidates are running as establishment or moderate Democrats and which candidates are running on progressive or socialist platforms. The left-wing label includes members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) like State Rep. Shaun Scott, progressive Democrats like Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal, Brent Hennrich, and Kevin Fagan, and independent left-wing candidates like Kshama Sawant and Melissa Chaudhry.

These primary results are evidence of what is already known in Olympia: that the governing Democratic Party in Washington State is a coalition of at least two smaller parties. Or, as Senate Majority Leader Jamie Pedersen put it on my podcast Ungerrymander America : “I’m already the leader of a multiparty coalition called the Democratic Party, that includes a broad range of people. From people who, if you could just get them to say what they think, identify as communists or socialists, to people who in a different time could easily have been Republicans, and everything in between.”

Though this emerging left-wing party is not yet formalized, candidates espousing anti-establishment, progressive, or socialist rhetoric and policies are finding support across the state. In addition to former Congressional Progressive Caucus chair Pramila Jayapal (WA-7), left-wing candidates received enough votes across Western Washington to prevent four incumbent Democratic Congresspeople from reaching 50% of the vote: Rick Larsen (WA-2), Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (WA-3), Adam Smith (WA-9), and Marilyn Strickland (WA-10).

Across the mountains in Eastern Washington's Fifth Congressional District, incumbent Republican Michael Baumgartner underperformed, receiving just 47.4% of the vote. The remaining 52.6% was split between mainstream Democrats, progressives, and independents.

Failing to win 50% of the vote means Baumgartner is vulnerable. But for challenger Carmela Conroy to win, she will need to build a cross-spectrum coalition that includes everyone from the 4.4% of voters who voted for left-wing candidates to the more than 20% of voters who voted independent. Conroy's coalition building efforts were helped by the full-throated endorsement of her by independent Nate Powell, who finished third with 16.5% of the primary vote.
Taken together, over one-quarter of primary voters voted for either a left-wing or independent alternative to the two-party system to represent them in Congress.
The same kind of multiparty dynamic is playing out in legislative races across Washington State.

First, contests in the 37th and 43rd districts show that Seattle has a two-party system of moderate/establishment Democrats being challenged by progressive Democrats and DSA-candidates. Both districts will send a DSA-member to the legislature, with the 43rd's Shaun Scott running unopposed for reelection and the 37th’s Jaelynn Scott winning an overwhelming 88% of the primary vote.

Both districts have contested races, with the establishment Democrat Sen. Jamie Pedersen favored to win reelection in the 43rd. On the other hand, left-wing challenger Kelabe Tewolde won more than 51% in the primary in the 37th. These results should not be interpreted as definitive victories for either the moderates or the progressives; the key takeaway is that there are two distinct factions competing across Seattle districts and the more left-leaning democratic socialist faction is making headway and establishing itself as a distinct political force.

This isn’t only playing out in Seattle. Left-wing candidates are making gains elsewhere too. In the redrawn 14 th district that stretches from Yakima to the Tri-Cities, incumbent Republican Rep. Deb Manjarrez received 51% of the primary vote, showing that the district will be competitive in November. In the race for second place, the labor and immigrant rights activist Ezequiel Morfin beat self-described moderate Tony G. Sandoval. To be clear, Morfin identifies as a Democrat. I categorize him as part of this emerging left-wing party because his platform centers working families and places his campaign in opposition to corporate donors and party insiders.

Meanwhile, voters in Eastern Washington are looking for independent alternatives. In addition to Nate Powell coming within 3% of second place in the Fifth Congressional District, the 6th Legislative District had independent Aaron Croft come within 259 votes of advancing to the general. Powell and Croft were two of five independent candidates in Eastern Washington endorsed by the Independent Veterans of America .

The concurrent and separate races for the two State House seats in the 6th LD show the appeal of independents. For seat #1, four Republicans combined for 57% of the vote while two Democrats received 42%. But just 50% of 6th LD voters supported Republican Jonathan Bingle for seat #2. Some 2,000 voters, 7% of the 6th LD primary electorate, voted Republican in one race then voted Independent in the other.

Take it all together and the shape of Washington’s multiparty politics comes into focus: the governing moderate to center-left Democrats fighting off a challenge from a left-wing party currently strong in Seattle and growing across the state; and a Republican Party losing relevancy in the State Legislature facing challenges from increasingly organized independent candidates.

Unfortunately, the structure of Washington’s top-two voting system is artificially keeping the two-party system in place and contributing to the widespread political cynicism that contributes to many people opting-out of voting. Voter turnout in the 2026 primary was just 37%, lower than the more than 40% turnout in midterm primaries in 2022 and 2018.

By implementing a proportional voting system, such as proportional ranked choice voting (RCV), Washington could send a multiparty delegation to Congress and have a formal multiparty politics in the State Legislature. This would help heal our political cynicism by providing voters real options beyond the two-party system.

Instead of a winner-take-all system like we have now, where the candidate with 50.1% of the vote wins and the other 49.9% of the district is left without, proportional RCV elects multiple winners in the same district. This means far more than 50% of voters will see someone they voted for win the election. For example, in a district where the top three candidates win, 75% of voters would be represented; in a four-winner district this goes up to 80%.

Individual candidates would still need to win at least 20% of the vote to be elected in a four-winner district. For a deep dive on the mechanics, see chapter 6 of my 2024 book Polemic for Democracy on the Ungerrymander America blog .
Finally, if implemented, the multiple winner function of proportional RCV makes gerrymandering functionally impossible , according to analysis by the Brennan Center for Justice.

Shifting to proportional RCV for electing members of the State House could be done through the normal legislative process, while changing the voting system for the Senate may require amending the state constitution ( Article 2, Section 6 ).

But, such a change may be unlikely to be popular among legislators bought into the existing two-party system. A final option if legislation for proportional RCV fails to gain traction in Olympia would be for Washington voters to bring an initiative to demand a better voting system that would give them more options.

The primary results show that at least 25% of voters are already putting their votes toward alternatives to the two-party status quo. And if there were a real chance to change the system? Who knows how broad the support for such an initiative might reach.

articles.title: Give Yourself Over to Absolute Pleasure at These ‘Rocky Horror’ Screenings
articles.author: Julianne Bell
paras: Tim Curry, known for his legendary performances in It , Clue , Home Alone 2, Legend , and The Rocky Horror Picture Show , died Tuesday night in his Los Angeles home. He was 80, and along with Dolly Parton, one of two gay icons to leave this world in a single day.

Like countless others, my strongest connection to Curry was through his portrayal of Dr. Frank-N-Furter—the “sweet transvestite from Transexual, Transylvania”—in Rocky Horror . As an (unknowingly) queer teen, wearing pleather and fishnets at midnight Rocky Horror screenings at the Admiral Theatre in West Seattle was a rite of passage. A few of my high school classmates were in the shadowcast, the costumed performers miming the action on screen. My mom went to screenings when she was young. Rocky Horror , and Curry, were always there.

Except—as my colleague, and fellow Rocky Horror devotee, Audrey Vann, lamented in our Complaints Issue last December —shadowcast performances seem to be nearly extinct in Seattle. Blessedly, for the sake of the youth, there are still a few. There’s no better time to do the Time Warp than where you are standing. Or, if you can wait, during the following shadowcast performances.

Riff Raff’s Street Rats is a Bremerton-based volunteer shadowcast troupe that performs at their home theater, the Tracyton Movie House, and at venues across the region, raising money for nonprofits across the Northwest. They have three shows planned in honor of Curry’s memory. See them tomorrow night (Saturday, August 29) at the Skyline Drive-In Theater in Shelton. Gates open at 7:30 p.m. Get there early for the 9 p.m. pre-show initiation ritual before the 9:30 p.m. screening. According to their website, audience “partici…… pation” is encouraged. The Street Rats next take the stage Saturday, September 19, at the Admiral Theater. Doors open at 9 p.m. and the show starts at 9:30 p.m. Their biggest Tim Curry tribute will take place at Olympia’s Capitol Theater on Saturday, October 3 , with doors at 11 p.m. and pre-show beginning at 11:30 p.m. before the film—a rare midnight screening. Prop bags will be sold separately outside the venue.

On Instagram , the Street Rats expressed their grief at Curry’s death. Says cast member Chynna: “Growing up in rural Idaho, there was very little support for the LGBTQ+ community. I had to hide who I was, who I liked, and what I wanted, until a beautiful man with a beautiful voice kicked in the door with platform heels. My world was rocked. To me, it did feel like being transported to another planet, and for once in my life, I did feel like I was coming home. Tim became a beacon of hope for me, a battle cry for everything I did that got me called ‘weird,’ and I am honored to still perform in the shadow of that greatness.”

Tacoma’s Blue Mouse Theater screens Rocky Horror every second and fourth Saturday of the month, with their in-house shadowcast, the BlueMouseketeers. On September 12, they’ll host a memorial for Curry . The cast will organize a small memorial altar outside the theater, and guests are invited to donate art, cards, or other small items in his memory. Concessions and prop bags will be available at the lobby. Doors open at 11 p.m.

“For decades, the Rocky Horror Picture Show has provided a space of community and belonging for people of all walks of life; notably, the queer and trans communities, and Curry has played a huge part in that,” the BlueMouseketeers wrote on Instagram . “In honor of Tim Curry, we ask you all to remember the movie’s message of ‘don’t dream it, be it.’ We can’t ever replace this loss, and it’s difficult to express in words the grief this community feels, but the Blue Mouseketeers are committed to carrying on Curry’s legacy and keeping this show alive for as long as we can.”

Another shadowcast, the Vicarious Theatre Company , performs at the downtown Regal Meridian 16 the first Saturday of every month. I couldn’t find any information about Curry tributes, but on the Regal website , a show is scheduled for 10 p.m. on Saturday, September 5.

Prior to Curry’s death, a few Rocky Horror events were already scheduled in Seattle for the Halloween season. Patricia Quinn, who played Magenta in the original film, will stop by the 5th Avenue Theater on Thursday, October 15 for the 7 p.m. Rocky Horror Picture Spooktacular Tour screening . The evening will feature a live shadowcast with the BlueMousketeers, plus a VIP meet-and-greet with photo ops and autographs. Obec Brewing will host an interactive singalong screening at 7 p.m. on Friday, October 30, while Unexpected Productions will put a live improv spin on the film each Saturday in October.

articles.title: When a mountain falls: How ice and rock triggered Nepal’s catastrophic flood – and why climate change is raising the risks
articles.author:
<name>Umesh Haritashya, Professor of Earth, Environment and Sustainability, and Director of Sustainability Programs, University of Dayton</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/umesh-haritashya-2761412"/>
paras: The catastrophic flood that killed hundreds of people in Nepal on Aug. 26, 2026, and left many more missing likely began with falling ice and rock crashing into the river below, but that wasn’t the end of the disaster. Days later, a new lake pooled behind the debris and then burst, sending more water streaming through the valley.

The destruction represents two of the ways rising temperatures, thawing permafrost and melting ice are increasing the risk of destructive floods in the Himalayas and other high mountain regions around the world.

I am a geologist and part of an ad hoc international group of 50-plus scientists who meet quickly after mountain disasters to analyze satellite images and field data to get information out to the public. This is what we’ve learned so far about the disaster and the region’s rising risks from climate change.

Evidence from satellites and seismic data we have reviewed suggest that an enormous mass of bedrock and glacier ice broke off a slope north of Langtang Lirung and slammed into the valley about 4,000 feet (1,200 meters) below – that’s a distance roughly three times the height of the Eiffel Tower. The landslide shook the earth hard enough to register as a magnitude 5.2 event on seismometers, the U.S. Geological Survey confirmed .
The result was a slurry of melting ice, rock and water that quickly flowed into the river.

We have a rough idea of how much ice fell, and it likely wouldn’t have been enough to trigger the magnitude of the flood that followed. One theory is that the rock and ice briefly dammed the valley , allowing water to back up in the river.
When that blockage broke, a wall of water rushed downstream – reaching towns, taking hundreds of lives and destroying infrastructure. Hundreds more people were stranded by the flood .

The disaster wasn’t finished when the first wall of water passed. Within a day, authorities warned that a new “ barrier lake ” estimated to hold a few million cubic meters of water had developed behind avalanche and flood debris where two rivers meet in Tibet, a region of China, before crossing into Nepal.

On Aug. 28, the barrier lake broke its bank and the river rose again. Helicopter search operations were briefly suspended while rescuers and residents on the lower banks scrambled to high ground. The immediate danger eased only when the barrier drained gradually rather than collapsing all at once.

This is the crux of why these events are so dangerous: A temporary, debris-choked dam can form in minutes, hold for hours or days, and fail with little warning. An avalanche-dammed lake often appears and disappears too quickly for conventional monitoring to catch.
We’re seeing disasters like this happen frequently.

In 2021, a similar rock and ice avalanche in India’s Uttarakhand state sent about 950 million cubic feet (27 million cubic meters) of rock and ice – roughly 80% rock, 20% ice – cascading down from Ronti Peak. It destroyed one hydropower plant, badly damaged another and killed or left missing about 200 people, many of them dam workers.

In 2025, roughly 335 million cubic feet (9.5 million cubic meters) of rock and ice fell from the Birch Glacier in the Swiss Alps, burying most of the village of Blatten; only advance monitoring and the evacuation of more than 300 residents kept the death toll to one.
The number of glacial lakes has also increased around the world, raising the risk of outburst floods. And more mountain slopes are now at risk of landslides than in the past.

In 2023, thawing permafrost led to a rock collapse into South Lhonak Lake in Sikkim, India, generating a wave that burst through the moraine holding back the glacial lake . The outburst flood sent more than 13 billion gallons (50 million cubic meters) of water rushing down the mountain, damaging several dams, more than 25,000 buildings and more than 30 bridges.
Climate change is one major contributor to rising disaster risk.
The last 10 years have been the warmest on record globally , and that has accelerated snow and glacier melt .

Populations are growing, too, and these valleys are increasingly being used to generate hydropower. As countries build more infrastructure in these places, the hazard risk rises because more people and development sit in the flood’s path.

The valley where the latest disaster occurred held multiple hydropower plants – Nepal’s electricity authority said the flood knocked about a dozen major generation and transmission facilities offline. Bridges and a major border crossing , the Gyirong Port gateway between Nepal and China, were also destroyed. It became a catastrophe because of where the water, rock and mud landed.

Together with the neighboring Hindu Kush mountains, the rugged Himalayas that stretch across Asia contain one of the world’s largest volumes of ice . They’re sometimes called the “third pole” for that reason.
As temperatures have risen, their ice loss rates roughly doubled since 2000, according to studies from the Nepal-based International Center for Integrated Mountain Development, or ICIMOD.

And it isn’t only the glaciers that are melting. High mountain slopes are also held together by permafrost – ground that stays frozen year-round – with ice filling the cracks and joints in the rock like a natural cement. As that frozen ground warms and ice inside thaws, the cement weakens, and slopes that stood for thousands of years can lose their grip.
Meltwater from snow and ice seeps into cracks in the rock. Where it refreezes, it can pry those cracks wider. Where it stays liquid, it acts as a lubricant along the surfaces where rock and ice meet.

On a steep cliff, these water-filled fractures can sometimes be the difference between a face that holds and one that gives way all at once – sending millions of tons of rock and ice into the valley below in seconds.

Not every thaw ends in disaster. But rising temperatures steadily load the dice: more slopes lose their frozen glue, more meltwater works its way into the cracks, and the odds of a catastrophic collapse rise year after year.
In the 2021 disaster in Uttarakhand, thawing likely contributed to the collapse of a large slab of rock and ice on the face of Ronti Peak.

Early indications in Nepal point to a similar story: a large mass of rock and ice detaching from a mountainside and falling, triggering the August 2026 flood. Comparing satellite images of the site from before and after , first posted by my colleague Dan Shugar , we have also noticed that a lot of snow had disappeared in the days preceding the flood. That snowmelt had to go somewhere – and it may have supplied the water that lubricated the rockfall.
From a risk standpoint, some areas of these mountains are extremely dangerous today.

To help protect people, early warning systems are crucial . When a flood starts, people living farther down the valley might have several minutes to get to safety before the water arrives – and minutes are enough to save lives.

Nepal has warning systems in place , and they have been credited with preventing casualties in the past. But the warning systems rely heavily on river-level gauges, which work far better for monsoon floods than for a wall of water moving tens of meters per second – and the flood itself likely destroyed the very gauges the warning systems depend on.

Building redundancy into the system would help, such as adding seismic sensors that detect a large mass movement the instant it happens, sirens and loudspeakers in valley-bottom settlements, radio and satellite-based cell broadcasts that don’t rely on a single tower that a flood can sweep away, and automatic alerts triggered when an avalanche and sudden water and sediment level in the river jumps.

Knowing the risks can also improve permit decisions for hydropower dams, roads and buildings in high-hazard corridors – and it can push monitoring beyond the familiar checklist of large glacial lakes to hanging glaciers, steep ice-and-rock slopes, permafrost, and the short-lived debris dams that can be just as deadly.

Regional cooperation is also important. When rivers cross borders or a transboundary glacial lake has potential to fail , the disaster doesn’t stop at the border. The water that devastated Nepal began on the Tibetan side, and the barrier lake that threatened a second surge sat right on the frontier.
Umesh Haritashya receives funding from NASA and other similar basic and applied Earth science research funding organizations.

articles.title: Game over, new routine: Laid-off Xbox manager built her Korean skincare startup before cuts hit
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Long before the July email arrived confirming she was one of thousands of Xbox employees laid off in Microsoft’s latest round of job cuts, Agnes Kim could feel the impending doom hanging over big tech.

But instead of waiting around for the next pendulum swing, the eight-year Xbox veteran spent her nights and weekends laying the groundwork for a very different kind of reboot: a boutique Korean skincare startup called ViaJiin .

The pivot from big tech and gaming to startups and beauty is an illustration in how preparation can help a laid off worker upend the usual five stages of grief that come before figuring out what to do next. Kim skipped straight to acceptance — announcing her new venture on LinkedIn just two days after getting her pink slip from Microsoft.

Kim joined the tech giant in 2018 after roles at Sony Pictures Entertainment and Deloitte Consulting, eventually rising to director leading Xbox’s market expansion in Asia. For years, she thrived in the role, building teams and expanding the gaming footprint in regions close to her roots. But as post-pandemic gaming demand normalized, the environment shifted from ambitious growth to what felt like a cycle of corporate survival.

Starting in early 2023, layoffs began rolling through the company every six months . Seeing the predictable pattern take its toll on team morale, Kim realized she couldn’t rely on long-term corporate stability to fulfill her goal of becoming an entrepreneur .
“You have a sense of impending doom,” Kim recalled. “There’s a shadow lurking. I felt like every six months we were waiting for the next round. I just didn’t feel like I was in an upswing anymore.”

Determined to take control of her timeline, she began tinkering with her business concept in late 2025, officially forming an LLC for ViaJiin in March 2026 and running focus groups by May — all while balancing her full-time executive role. When the July cuts finally hit Xbox, eliminating 1,600 jobs , Kim had already built six months of momentum.

Kim’s connection to skincare is deeply personal, rooted in her childhood spent living in South Korea from ages eight to 15. She grew up watching her mother religiously follow a multi-step routine and stress the daily necessity of sunscreen — a reflection of a culture where maintaining a youthful appearance carries immense social expectation.

That intense domestic demand has birthed a fiercely competitive market of over 30,000 brands, driving rapid scientific innovation. It has also turned South Korea into a global beauty powerhouse, with cosmetics exports surging past $10 billion as the U.S. recently surpassed China as the top destination for Korean beauty products.

ViaJiin aims to solve the overwhelming paralysis that American consumers face when trying to navigate the K-beauty market. Instead of building a massive retail catalog or pushing complicated 12-step routines, Kim simplifies the process into a streamlined four-product kit — cleanser, toner, serum, and cream — curated through a digital skin quiz. And she bypasses mainstream brands sold at big-box retailers to source exclusively from boutique Korean makers.
“The products I carry, you can only get through me,” Kim said. “I find boutique products that are filled with good ingredients, come to the U.S. compliantly, and turn it into a kit.”

ViaJiin’s full kits sell for $179, while smaller duo sets are priced at $99. Since shipping her first orders in August, Kim has been hand-packing boxes herself with personalized touches, building early traction online while hosting small, local events like “ViaJiin Nights” to let clients test products in person. The kits have also secured retail shelf space at K-Beauty & Skin in Renton, Wash., where Kim lives.
Kim’s transition from managing corporate teams to operating as a solo founder has meant trading human delegation for AI assistance.

Toward the end of her tenure at Microsoft, every conversation and initiative was dominated by a relentless push toward AI. Kim is now embracing those tools to execute work that would typically require a suite of employees or contractors.

She’s relied on Anthropic’s Claude as a virtual strategist and used platforms like Lovable to try her hand at “vibe coding” — the trend of using conversational natural-language prompts to generate functional software code — building out ViaJiin’s website and skin quiz without hiring a developer.
“I don’t have a co-founder… I’m delegating to Claude and GPT,” Kim said. “People are very surprised by my website or the skin quiz. I’m not an engineer, but it looks like I hired a web designer.”

While AI can handle code and logistics prompts, Kim quickly found that software can only go so far when running a physical inventory business. Between navigating complex U.S. FDA labeling regulations, managing customs paperwork, and verifying ingredient compliance, the operational heavy lifting remains resolutely analog.
And the shift from corporate structure to total solitary accountability is daunting at times.
Without a team to delegate to or a clear roadmap of objectives and key results, Kim admits there are moments where the freedom of entrepreneurship gives way to self-doubt.

“I think I understand why some people just work for the man,” Kim joked. “When you work for Microsoft, certainty and structure are more there. There are definitely moments where I’m like, ‘What the f*ck am I doing? What is today’s goal?'”

Still, Kim has no interest in turning back. Energized by the daily hustle and the creative control of building something from scratch, she insists she wouldn’t trade the experience for her old corporate desk. She hopes to grow ViaJiin into a household national brand while staying out of big tech for as long as she can.
“I’m 1,000% energized. I absolutely would not trade it,” Kim said. “This is allowing me to be truly the version of Agnes that I thought I would be when I was 12, and I want to keep going at it.”

articles.title: UW AI researcher wins top Marconi award and aims to put ‘superhuman hearing’ in billions of devices
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: University of Washington Ph.D. student Malek Itani , who co-founded the AI-powered sound enhancement startup Hearvana , has been awarded the prestigious Marconi Society Paul Baran Young Scholar Award for his groundbreaking work in “superhuman” hearing technology.

Selected as one of just three global recipients from a record pool of nominees, Itani was recognized for developing on-device AI algorithms that enable real-time target speech extraction, “sound bubbles,” and semantic hearing on low-power hearables like earbuds and hearing aids.

Itani’s award comes less than a year after he and Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering professor Shyam Gollakota co-founded Hearvana, a spinout aimed at commercializing their lab discoveries. The startup raised $6 million in pre-seed funding last fall to bring on-device acoustic intelligence to earbuds, hearing aids, and smart glasses.

By packing tiny, real-time neural networks onto low-power chips, the researchers hope to replace blunt noise cancellation with true semantic hearing — allowing users to filter out city traffic, amplify a single companion’s voice in a crowded room, or create a localized “sound bubble” on demand.

Itani’s work in the UW Mobile Intelligence Lab began with “acoustic swarms” — small, self-distributing robotic microphones that track and separate multiple speakers in a room. He and his collaborators then pivoted to personal audio devices, pioneering neural networks like IF-MLPNet and platforms like NeuralAids. These systems allow complex AI models to handle real-time sound separation directly on low-power wireless hearables without relying on heavy cloud compute or draining battery life.

“Malek has been a key part of every major contribution to the field of superhuman hearing in recent years,” Gollakota told the Allen School Blog . “He entered his Ph.D. with a background in RF and backscatter, but he rapidly mastered audio signal processing and deep learning, which is very impressive.”
“I feel like I’ve hit a niche that’s going to be so transformational, and it’s going to be in billions of devices,” Itani said. “It’s going to change the way we hear the world.”
Itani and his fellow Young Scholars will be formally recognized at the Marconi Awards Gala in San Francisco this November.

articles.title: Pro.com co-founders reunite to launch OnTrade, an AI startup for the wealth management industry
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: The co-founders of Pro.com, the Seattle-based home-improvement marketplace acquired by Opendoor in 2021, are back with a new company targeting what seems on the surface a very different kind of market: AI-powered software for the wealth management industry.

But Rajalakshmi “Raji” Subramanian and Matt Williams say the new challenge matches the same pattern: a huge industry held back not by a lack of customers, but by a shortage of professionals and tools.

Their Seattle startup, OnTrade , co-founded with former Bank of America chief investment officer Zachary Harl , has been operating under the radar since 2024, raising an undisclosed amount of funding from General Catalyst, Madrona and angel investors.
OnTrade’s chief technology officer is Jean Bredeche , who co-founded Quantopian, the algorithmic trading platform, and later served as a director of engineering at Robinhood.
How it works: OnTrade connects software that financial advisors already use — including CRM, portfolio accounting, trading, and compliance programs — into a single interface.

It then deploys AI agents to handle the type of work that advisors have traditionally done manually, such as scanning portfolios for tax-loss harvesting opportunities, flagging accounts that have drifted from their targets, or drafting proposals and reports for clients.

The humans approve everything before it reaches a client. The idea is to help them serve more clients without sacrificing the quality of their work, expanding access to wealth-management services that tend to be concentrated among more affluent households.

“Wealth management, if you look at the industry, does not have a demand problem; it has an access problem,” said Subramanian, the company’s CEO, in an interview. “Many people who’d like access to wealth management don’t have access to wealth management, and that’s what we’re here to solve.”

Harl, OnTrade’s chief investment officer, called raw foundation models the “brilliant PhDs” of the AI world — impressive on paper, but not as valuable to a specific industry such as wealth management until they understand its portfolios, policies, compliance rules, and client relationships. Vertical AI solutions like OnTrade, he said, are better positioned to connect that general-purpose intelligence to a specific firm’s data and workflows so the technology can do trusted work.

Industry shakeup: OnTrade is emerging at a pivotal moment, two days after investment giant Vanguard agreed to acquire wealth-management platform Altruist reportedly valued at $4 billion . OnTrade’s founders cite the deal as validation of the vertical AI opportunity they’re pursuing.

In a LinkedIn post Thursday, Subramanian wrote that the Vanguard-Altruist deal signals something bigger than a battle over where advisors park their clients’ assets: that capturing the opportunity “requires a new operating model rather than AI-enhanced versions of today’s applications.”
The wealth management industry’s unit of scale, she wrote, is shifting “from the number of people a firm employs to the intelligence and agency it can deploy.”
The founders: Subramanian joined Amazon in the late 1990s as an early engineer who helped build Amazon Marketplace and AWS, and later led the digitization of books for Kindle.

Amazon was where she met Williams, who had founded a startup called LiveBid that Amazon acquired in 1999. He spent 11 years there, including a stint as a technical advisor to Jeff Bezos, then left to run Digg as CEO and served as an entrepreneur in residence at Andreessen Horowitz.

Subramanian went on to run engineering at Yahoo Finance, where she helped open up market data that had previously been the province of institutional investors, giving her an early look at the problem that OnTrade is now aiming to solve.
In 2013, the two co-founded Pro.com, a tech-driven home improvement marketplace that raised early funding from investors including Madrona, Maveron, Bezos and Andreessen Horowitz.

Real estate tech company Opendoor acquired Pro.com in 2021 , and brought both founders on as executives — Subramanian as chief technology officer, Williams as head of the Pro.com unit and senior vice president of retail.

Harl spent many years at Bank of America, rising to chief investment officer, where he managed the bank’s asset portfolios and large balance sheet risks across multiple market cycles. He is a chartered financial analyst (CFA), with a math and computer science degree from Indiana University, and a statistics degree from the London School of Economics.

He served on the U.S. Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee under Secretaries Steven Mnuchin and Janet Yellen, advising on debt management, before joining Opendoor in 2023 as chief risk officer. That’s where he met Subramanian and Williams, before making the startup leap with them.
Traction and competition: The company’s technology is already in use at firms ranging in size from boutique advisories to large national practices, said Williams, the company’s president.

He said one client used the platform to win a billion-dollar family office account, and that another recouped the full annual cost of the platform in less than 30 days. He called that “a small window into what’s going to happen on a larger scale.”

The wealth management software market has many established players — such as Orion Advisor Solutions, Envestnet, and Addepar — but the OnTrade founders say they see them as partners, not rivals. OnTrade integrates with those systems rather than replacing them.

That distinguishes the company from Altruist, the Vanguard acquisition target, which built its own full stack, including its own custodian, the financial institution where client assets are held. That approach requires firms to move client assets onto its platform.
OnTrade doesn’t ask firms to replace their existing tools or move their clients’ money. Instead, it plugs into what’s already there.

The broader timing may work in their favor. As baby boomers age, an estimated $50 trillion or more in assets is expected to pass to younger generations in the coming decades — creating a wave of new clients who will need financial advisors, and new pressure on firms to serve them.
That’s where home improvement and wealth management have something in common.

“There aren’t many bigger places, other than health, wealth and real estate, where you can impact a population, especially an underserved population,” Williams said. “That was at the heart of the motivation.”

articles.title: Seattle startup Arkero expands English soccer reach, landing historic club as latest AI customer
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Arkero , a Seattle-area startup leveraging AI to help professional sports teams streamline business operations, has expanded its reach in English soccer by landing Bolton Wanderers FC as its latest client .
The agreement builds on momentum for Arkero, which was launched last fall by the co-founder of Seattle digital remittance company Remitly and raised $6 million at the start of this year.

Bolton Wanderers — which earned promotion back to the English Championship in May — joins a client roster that includes Major League Soccer’s Seattle Sounders FC, NWSL’s Seattle Reign FC, MLS expansion team San Diego FC, and fifth-tier English side Southend United.

The project with Bolton centers on a three-month effort to overhaul the team’s data infrastructure and build a custom “club intelligence layer.” Designed to connect directly to Bolton’s internal data, systems, and workflows, the platform centralizes organizational knowledge so staff across business and football operations can query information and deploy practical AI tools and agents.

“AI transformation does not begin with a chatbot. It begins with a club’s data, systems, knowledge and workflows,” said Shivaas Gulati, founder and CEO of Arkero, in a news release on Friday. “The future football workplace will bring experienced people and AI systems together. Bolton has approached this work with real ambition.”

Gulati’s drive to apply AI to sports comes directly from his own ties to the game. He serves on the ownership group of Southend United and previously acted as a technical advisor to Sounders FC on its tech and AI strategy.

“We get to see the real problems inside sports teams given our access to Southend United,” Gulati told GeekWire. “Clubs have been doing things the same way for a long time, and with AI they can truly re-imagine how their workforce operates and adapts to the demands of a modern enterprise.”

A longtime angel investor, Gulati co-founded Remitly in 2011 and left in 2022. He launched Arkero with help from Vamsi Narla , who leads product and engineering, and Daniel Shi , who oversees business operations. The startup has eight full-time employees.

Based in Greater Manchester, Bolton Wanderers boasts a rich legacy as one of the 12 founding members of the English Football League in 1888. Originally formed in 1874 as Christ Church F.C., the historic club has won four FA Cups and spent over 70 seasons in English football’s top flight.

Bolton CEO David Ray said the club is making a long-term investment to ensure it isn’t “playing catch-up” as technology reshapes the sports industry. The club aims to use Arkero’s platform to drive revenue, streamline administrative tasks, and better engage fans — joining teams like the Sounders and Reign, which project over 50% efficiency savings in matchday planning using the startup’s tools.

Arkero says interest in its deep AI integration model is accelerating across the sports world. The startup is currently in discussions with multiple English Football League clubs as well as professional sports teams and leagues across Europe and North America, as leadership teams seek to move beyond generic AI tools and connect AI directly to their proprietary data and daily workflows.

“There is a window right now for forward-thinking clubs to build a meaningful advantage,” Gulati said. “In a few years, working alongside AI will simply be how professional sports organizations operate.”

articles.title: Everett Link Reaches Key Federal Approval Milestone
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The Federal Transit Administration (FTA) has put its signature on the draft environmental analysis for Sound Transit's Everett Link project, which would extend light rail 16 miles north from Lynnwood.

Board Vice Chair Ryan Mello shared the news at the Sound Transit board meeting Thursday, noting federal approval allows the project to tick off another milestone. Sound Transit is aiming to open Everett Link in two phases, with four stations up to SW Industrial Center tentatively set for 2037, and Downtown Everett tabbed for 2041.

"Last week, we received some outstanding news from our federal partners, as the Federal Transit Administration signed the Everett Link Extension Draft Environmental Impact Statement, clearing the way for a September 18th publication of that really important extension," Mello said. "This is a key milestone. It launches the public engagement period for Everett Link Extension, in which the region will be able to learn more about the current state of the project, and share their priorities for Everett Link Extension going forward."
The public engagement period on Everett Link will start on September 18 as soon as the draft Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) is released and must last at least 45 days by law.

The draft EIS will need to be finalized and converted into a final EIS, which will also require federal approval and another public comment period. With that hurdle cleared, Sound Transit could advance to final designs and break ground on the project.

Sound Transit is still waiting on FTA approval to release the DEIS for the much more complex Ballard Link Extension. Originally, that document was initially set to be released much earlier than the Everett Link counterpart. The agency blames "federal regulatory changes" since the second Trump Administration took office, with every additional month of delay on that project costing the agency tens of millions according to Sound Transit.
The release of Everett Link's DEIS suggests that not all projects are receiving the same level of scrutiny and headwinds at the FTA.

Sound Transit is hoping to wrap planning on Everett Link by the end of 2027, with construction anticipated to start in early 2031. That timeline makes the project somewhat less at the whims of the Trump Administration, which has yet to sign any transit grant agreements since taking office in 2025 – in fact it has sought to claw back several existing transit grants – even as it has been willing to eventually approve some transit planning documents. A new administration that could take over in 2029 may be friendlier.

Advancing the Everett extension has been a clear priority for the agency's 18-member board, under the banner of " completing the spine " from Tacoma Dome to Everett Station, a 62-mile corridor. This is especially true for the board's Snohomish County delegation led by Snohomish County Executive Dave Somers, who chairs the board.

Hooking over to SW Industrial Center is far from the most direct route to downtown Everett, but it does take the light rail line near Paine Field – which Snohomish County officials hope to grow into a secondary airport for the region —plus Boeing's sprawling manufacturing plant. This preference has led the board to rule out the cheaper, faster alignments along SR 99 or I-5.

Voters approved funding for Everett Link in 2016's Sound Transit 3 (ST3) ballot measure, but most projects in that package have run into significant planning hurdles. Back in 2016, Sound Transit had hoped to open Tacoma Dome Link in 2030 and Everett Link in 2036, while West Seattle Link was tabbed for 2030 and Ballard Link for 2035.
A 2021 ST3 realignment delayed timelines for most projects, with the pandemic taking a good chunk of the blame.

In May, the board overhauled ST3 delivery schedules in light of a $34.5 billion long-term budget gap. The "Affordable ST3 Plan" put forward by Chair Somers delayed several extensions, potentially scrapping some projects forever. However, Everett Link made it out relatively unscathed, with no further delays announced at the time.

The Tacoma Dome Link Extension is still officially tabbed for 2035 , but with Sound Transit not anticipating breaking ground until 2030, that could be optimistic. The construction phase on Sound Transit's light rail projects have generally lasted six years or more .

In contrast, the agency revealed last month light rail to Ballard could be pushed to 2060s without further action to find major savings or secure new revenue. The agency's best-case scenario would open the entire Ballard Link project from SoDo to Ballard in 2042, if it's able to close the roughly $8 billion budget gap that pushed it to table the Ballard and Interbay stations, while advancing the downtown segment.
The Everett Link project will need to keep moving through the process for its anticipated 2037 opening for the Paine Field segment to stay in play.

articles.title: New permit filings revive McDonald’s plans on Capitol Hill — UPDATE
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Paperwork rumors early this year of a McDonald’s coming to Broadway across from Capitol Hill Station were half-baked and incomplete. New filings are now turning up the heat — and adding an interesting late-summer side dish to what might come next at the busy intersection of Broadway, John, and E Olive Way including a possible big change for the neighborhood’s Trader Joe’s .
UPDATE : TJ’s is not involved in the project. See details below.

Tuesday, a Building & Land Use Pre-Application was filed for the former Rite Aid building for a tenant remodel of the long-shuttered space. The signee on the financial responsibility filing for a pre-application coaching process is a project manager for the burger giant. Her Linked In updates include posts celebrating “new store” McDonald’s openings across the country.

There’s even more. A second related filing describes a “Trader Joe’s Tenant Improvement and Expansion” project at the same address. That filing came from an advisor for the grocery chain whose name has also appeared on market projects in other cities including Portland.
He is also, curiously enough, the listed applicant for the McDonald’s paperwork.

For now, the only company with their name on the line is McDonald’s but we’re following up to find out if Trader Joe’s could also be in the mix — or if the advisor simply left an old project name on a template when submitting the applications for the burger chain.

While there is no record of any previous joint McDonald’s-Trader Joe’s joint development in the country, some kind of link-up might make sense at the corner to fill the large space. The 5,000-square-foot former pharmacy has been marketed for lease along with another 2,200-square-feet in the building. Trader Joe’s operating two markets on Capitol Hill in such close proximity would be highly unlikely.

UPDATE : CHS is told by a person with knowledge of the project that Trader Joe’s is not involved in the planning. A filing inadvertently included the chain’s name and has since been corrected in the city permit system.

The long ago Broadway Theater building has been empty since 2023 as a wave of bankruptcy shut down big-chain pharmacies across the city. In February , CHS joined a wave of media speculation after an early McDonald’s paperwork filing.
The area has been without a nearby source of Big Macs since the First Hill McDonald’s served its final fries in 2017 to make way for new development.

The Broadway building remains held by its longtime family ownership. McDonald’s typically signs long-term leases for its locations in urban neighborhoods and business districts, subleasing the spaces to franchisees.
CHS has questions out to relevant parties including the building’s longtime ownership. The Daily Journal of Commerce is also reporting on the filings.

articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: A recall effort over public safety policies against first-year Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson turned out to be a real nothingburger.

The applicants behind the filing withdrew their charges in a status conference this week, court officials said. The required public hearing on the charges was scheduled for Monday in King County Superior Court to determine if signature gathering to place a recall on the ballot could proceed.

The backdown by the Seattle-resident couple behind the filing followed allegations that Wilson has been derelict in her duties concerning public safety across the city, citing her policies around Seattle Police Department surveillance cameras, street disorder in areas like Aurora Ave and the International District, and her decision to demand the resignation of Chief Shon Barnes following the fatal shootout at the Bite of Seattle .
Despite threats, recall efforts in Seattle have been relatively rare. In 2021 , District 3 voters narrowly defeated a recall campaign against City Councilmember Kshama Sawant .

articles.title: Right-Wing Radio Host Ari Hoffman Files Political Finance Complaints Against the Seattle Times
articles.author: John Stang
paras: Radio host Ari Hoffman of KVI AM 570 news radio fired the first shot Aug.18 in a barrage of complaints to the state government that allege “the legacy media” is cheating on Washington’s campaign finance laws.
His target? The Seattle Times and its opposition to a failed 2024 ballot measure to repeal a new industrial carbon emissions law.
He filed his complaint against the Times and its Climate Lab with the Public Disclosure Commission, which regulates political campaign finances in Washington.

On Aug. 24, Hoffman filed a second PDC complaint regarding the Times’ project homelessness coverage, which has at least two reporters funded by donations from homeless institutions. He claims this coverage improperly boosted a Seattle housing property tax levy in 2023, which successfully replaced an expiring 2016 levy.
Hoffman declined comment. “I do not give comments to anti-American antisemitic rags like the Stranger,” he wrote in an email.

Essentially, Hoffman’s Climate Lab complaint to the PDC claims that liberal groups sent money to the Times through the Seattle Foundation—an 80-year-old philanthropic organization that provides grants and investment money to a wide range of causes and ventures, including donations it funnels to the Seattle Times ’ Climate Lab project—so the paper would write stories and editorials to sway readers to vote against a 2024 ballot measure that would repeal the state’s new Climate Commitment Act (CCA). The CCA, a quarterly state auction of carbon carbon emissions credits to polluting industries which pays for numerous global warming mitigation programs, survived by a 62-percent-to-38-percent margin.
The Seattle Foundation and some of the Climate Lab donors also make political donations.

According to Hoffman’s complaint, The Seattle Times and donor organizations should be investigated for potentially violating Washington campaign finance reporting requirements by not reporting the financial value and sponsor identification for political advertising, expenditures, contributions, and in-kind support associated with opposing 2024’s ballot measure.

The complaint claims the Climate Lab, a team of four climate reporters whose 2024 coverage specifically addressed the carbon emissions credits law only a handful of times, differs from normal newsroom operations because it is funded through donations and not from the paper’s normal revenue.

Hoffman wants the PDC to interview the Times ’s Climate Lab reporters and editorial board members. Plus, he wants the commission to examine all of the Times ’s stories and editorials, as well as all finances and emails involving the Times ’s relations with the Seattle Foundation and its climate-related donors.
The Seattle Times and the Seattle Foundation both declined comment.
Hoffman, a right-wing commentator, does not present any specific details that prove that the Times ’s climate change coverage is not factually based, accurate, nor objective.
This practice of using donations to bolster news coverage has become more common among newspapers, whose revenues have dramatically shrunk due to advertising drying up

The Spokesman-Review is one such paper. Its longtime owners—the Cowles family—recently transferred ownership to a new Spokane non-profit corporation, Comma Community Journalism Lab. Comma’s list of donors is public .

Also, the Washington State Standard is part of States Newsroom , a nationwide non-profit collection of newsrooms funded by roughly 1,200 donations of more than $1,000 for it to cover state governments. Conservative interests have accused States Newsroom of liberal biases, which the national organization denies having. The liberal Hopewell Fund largely bankrolled States Newsroom from 2017 to 2019 until the organization got on its feet. Several liberal interests are among the national group’s donors.
The Washington State Standard has the biggest statehouse news operation in Olympia, and is a neutral workhorse whose stories are reprinted by several state papers.

Another relatively new Olympia news operation funded solely by donors is The Center Square. The conservative Franklin News Foundation (formerly the Franklin Center) funds The Center Square in numerous states. Most donors to the Franklin News Foundation are anonymous. The Center Square (formerly Watchdog) concentrates on business and tax issues, although it has stretched into other matters.

Philanthropy.org, a nationwide donation-tracking Web site, says that Project 42, a leading Washington conservative funding operation, donated $3.1 million to the Franklin News Foundation from 2021 to 2024.

Redmond hedge fund manager Brian Heywood leads Let’s Go Washington, which has three initiatives on the November ballot – banning transgender girls from girls sports, revoking the millionaires’ income tax, and a parental rights measure.

Heywood also helps control the pursestrings of Project 42, whose subsidiary Future 42 is a regular advertiser on Brandi Kruse’s podcast. Kruse is also an official “ambassador” of Future 42, which translates to being a very vocal supporter.

Meanwhile, right-wing podcaster Kruse says she soon plans to file PDC complaints similar to Hoffman’s against the Times , the Tacoma News Tribune , The Stranger , her former employer KIRO Newsradio, and the independent Black outlet Converge Media.

Kruse and Hoffman are not coordinating their complaints. “Ari Hoffman did that all on his lonesome. I learned about it after the fact,” she said about his first complaint in an email to The Stranger .

Hoffman’s and Kruse’s PDC filings are apparent payback for a group called Washingtonians For Ethical Government (WFEG) filing a complaint against Let’s Go Washington in May. That complaint alleged that the conservative initiative organization Let’s Go Washington has not properly filed campaign documentation related to Kruse’s podcast, unDivided, being a major supporter of the organization’s November 2026 ballot measure to ban transgender girls from girls sports.

The WFEG complaint alleges 159 instances of Kruse boosting the measure on her podcast from September 2025 to February 2026, plus two times she led political rallies on the same topic. The complaint alleges that Kruse’s support crossed the line from commentary to at least $345,000 in free advertising. Kruse still discusses this measure on her podcast several times a week.
The PDC recently decided to launch a formal investigation into this claim—roughly 90 days after it was submitted. A couple Seattle television newsrooms noted that launch .
On her Aug. 18 podcast, Kruse pointed to the PDC not terminating the May complaint, which she contended unfairly tainted her and Let’s Go Washington with a bad image.

She believes that the PDC is deliberately not resolving the May complaint by now. “The PDC’s decision to allow (the Washingtonians For Ethical Government complaint) to linger is a political decision,” Kruse said.

As the PDC investigates the complaint against Let’s Go Washington, it will have to parse legal and semantic differences between commentary and free political advertising. A 2007 Washington Supreme Court ruling that declares radio host commentary is not political advertising will also likely be a factor in the PDC’s investigation. The commission will also likely examine financial and organizational ties between Kruse and Brian Heywood, sponsor of the anti-trans Let’s Go Washington measure and two others on November’s ballot.

Kruse is angry that her podcast is receiving bad publicity from this matter because Let’s Go Washington is accused of the actual insufficient campaign reporting – with her podcast not being required to report to the PDC. “I have a First Amendment right to support any initiative I choose,”she wrote in her email.

On her Aug. 18 podcast, Kruse said she would “assemble an army” to be paid with her own money to compile detailed information on the advertisers, stories and finances of The Seattle Times , The Stranger , The News Tribune , KIRO News Radio and Converge Media to send detailed complaints to the PDC.

Meanwhile, Kruse wrote in her email: “I selected a wide array of media outlets to make a point: it’s not about politics, it’s about equal treatment under the law. If the PDC chooses to erode my First Amendment rights, then they must also go after those who are similarly situated – including dear friends of mine. Anyone who engaged in commercial advertising while also engaging in opinion on candidates or campaigns is impacted.”
After the first five complaints are filed, Kruse plans to continue submitting similar complaints regarding other Washington news operations.
“I will spend every waking hour burying the PDC in bullshit over this,” she said on her Aug. 17 podcast.

Kruse and Hoffman ally themselves with right-wing activist Jonathan Choe. The trio routinely participate in conservative political activities. Kruse also is paid to speak at Republican functions, and she campaigned for free for GOP gubernatorial candidate David Reichert in 2024.

Months ago, Kruse and Cho attended an Antifa roundtable at the White House where Kruse told President Donald Trump that her support for his second term made her feel more attractive—a remark out of sync with accepted press professionalism.

The three are co-plaintiffs in a federal lawsuit to be declared journalists so they can get access to the Democratic side of the Capitol’s House chamber in Olympia. They already have access to the entire Senate chamber and to the GOP side of the House chamber by various means. The judge in charge of that litigation told them that their chances of prevailing in that lawsuit are slim.
While this is technically a separate issue from the PDC matter, Kruse has loosely co-mingled the two in a few podcasts.

Editor’s note: The original headline of this story read, “Right-Wing Podcaster Ari Hoffman Files Political Finance Complaints Against the Seattle Times.” While Ari Hoffman’s show is available to us all in podcast form, he is a radio host.
